chunks.section: Stochastic Projections and Rank-Aware Learning Rates for Federated LoRA
chunks.text: Saber Malekmohammadi Affiliation: Stanford University Email: sabermm@stanford.edu Kevin Kuo Affiliation: Carnegie Mellon University Email: kkuo2@andrew.cmu.edu Virginia Smith Affiliation: Carnegie Mellon University Email: smithv@cmu.edu Golnoosh Farnadi Affiliation: McGill University, MILA Email: farnadig@mila.quebec

Fine-tuning large-scale foundation models across resource-constrained, distributed clients presents significant computational and communication challenges. While merging Low-Rank Adaptation ( LoRA ) with Federated Learning ( FL ) enables rank-based flexibility, the interdependence of the adaptation matrices ( 𝐀 \mathbf{A} and 𝐁 \mathbf{B} ) often complicates optimization. In this work, we theoretically demonstrate that LoRA fine-tuning with Gaussian initialization and a frozen 𝐀 \mathbf{A} matrix acts as a stochastic approximation of full fine-tuning, where batch gradients are subject to a random, rank-dependent perturbation. Motivated by this insight, we propose freezing and periodically resampling 𝐀 \mathbf{A} matrices at the client level. This strategy decouples the 𝐀 \mathbf{A} and 𝐁 \mathbf{B} gradients, diminishes LoRA low-rank constraints and reduces both computational and uplink communication overheads by 50%, allowing for the reallocation of resources toward higher adaptation ranks. Furthermore, we show that in this frozen- 𝐀 \mathbf{A} regime, the adaptation rank r r directly governs the signal-to-noise ratio ( SNR ) of the perturbed gradients. Specifically, we find that the SNR increases linearly with r r , implying that clients’ learning rates must be dynamically scaled with their adaptation ranks for higher utility. Building on these foundations, we introduce SPRA-LoRA ( S tochastic P rojection and R ank- A ware LoRA ), a federated rank-aware fine-tuning strategy that utilizes frozen, resampled 𝐀 \mathbf{A} matrices and rank-dependent learning rates for clients. We also prove its convergence with heterogeneous client resources. Our experiments across benchmark datasets demonstrate that SPRA-LoRA consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines with half

Adapting foundation models (e.g., GPT [ 1 ] , BERT [ 2 ] and ViT [ 3 ] ) to downstream tasks requires the use of fine-tuning datasets that are often unavailable to or represented by just a single client. Federated learning ( FL ) [ 4 ] addresses this by enabling collaborative fine-tuning across multiple clients in a privacy-preserving manner. Despite the promise of FL , the large number of parameters in foundation models can make federated fine-tuning expensive. To reduce the computational and communication costs of federated fine-tuning, Parameter Efficient Fine-Tuning ( PEFT ) methods [ 5 , 6 , 7 ] freeze most pre-trained parameters, updating only a small subset. Specifically, LoRA [ 7 ] is a popular PEFT technique that has been integrated with FedAvg [ 4 ] for federated fine-tuning of LLM s [ 8 ] . LoRA formulates the update to an adapter 𝐖 0 ∈ ℝ n × m \mathbf{W}^{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times m} of a pre-trained model as 𝐖 = 𝐖 0 + s ​ 𝐁𝐀 \mathbf{W}=\mathbf{W}^{0}+s\mathbf{B}\mathbf{A} , where 𝐁 ∈ ℝ n × r , 𝐀 ∈ ℝ r × m \mathbf{B}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times r},\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times m} are matrices of rank r r and r ≪ min ⁡ { m , n } r\ll\min\{m,n\} . Also, s = α / r ν s=\alpha/r^{\nu} is a scaling factor, where α \alpha is a hyperparameter. This reduces the number of trainable parameters from m ​ n mn to r ⁡ ( m + n ) r(m+n) , making the rank r r a key hyperparameter for controlling client-side computational and communication costs in federated fine-tuning.

Various strategies have been adopted in the literature to combine LoRA with FL . Some works directly apply the FedAvg algorithm [ 4 ] to the LoRA components 𝐀 \mathbf{A} and 𝐁 \mathbf{B} and average them on the server as 𝐀 = ∑ i w i ​ 𝐀 i \mathbf{A}=\sum_{i}w_{i}\mathbf{A}_{i} and 𝐁 = ∑ i w i ​ 𝐁 i \mathbf{B}=\sum_{i}w_{i}\mathbf{B}_{i} , where w i w_{i} is the aggregation weight assigned to client i i [ 8 ] . However, noting that LoRA models the adapter update as Δ ​ 𝐖 = 𝐬𝐁𝐀 \Delta\mathbf{W=s\mathbf{B}\mathbf{A}} , this aggregation strategy suffers from an aggregation noise [ 9 , 10 ] rooted in the fact that: ( ∑ i w i ​ 𝐁 i ) ​ ( ∑ i w i ​ 𝐀 i ) ≠ ∑ i w i ​ Δ ​ 𝐖 i = ∑ i w i ​ ( s i ​ 𝐁 i ​ 𝐀 i ) . \displaystyle\big(\sum_{i}w_{i}\mathbf{B}_{i}\big)\big(\sum_{i}w_{i}\mathbf{A}_{i}\big)\neq\sum_{i}w_{i}\Delta\mathbf{W}_{i}=\sum_{i}w_{i}(s_{i}\mathbf{B}_{i}\mathbf{A}_{i}). (1) To address the aggregation noise, existing methods either 1) alternatingly update 𝐀 i \mathbf{A}_{i} and 𝐁 i \mathbf{B}_{i} (between clients’ local optimization steps or between communication rounds) and aggregate them separately [ 11 , 12 ] (this requires uniform ranks across clients), or 2) simultaneously update both and aggregate the resulting adapter updates { Δ ​ 𝐖 i } = { s i ​ 𝐁 i ​ 𝐀 i } \{\Delta\mathbf{W}_{i}\}=\{s_{i}\mathbf{B}_{i}\mathbf{A}_{i}\} [ 9 , 10 ] .

We demonstrate that both the above methods are sub-optimal. The first approach wastes significant client computation and communication on fine-tuning/transmitting the 𝐀 i \mathbf{A}_{i} matrices, which we show, for Gaussian-initialized LoRA , function more as random gradient perturbations than as essential knowledge-storing parameters. The second approach, while solving the aggregation noise problem, suffers from a gradient coupling issue between the 𝐀 \mathbf{A} and 𝐁 \mathbf{B} matrices: the current gradient update of 𝐀 \mathbf{A} depends on the current 𝐁 \mathbf{B} , and vice versa. Hence, when fine-tuned simultaneously , one matrix adapts to a basis that the other has already shifted away from and this induces the gradient coupling noise [ 12 ] . While the aforementioned alternate optimization of the two matrices can avoid this noise [ 12 , 11 ] , it spends half of the computation/communication resources of each client i i on fine-tuning/transmitting its 𝐀 i \mathbf{A}_{i} matrix. By avoiding the noise via freezing matrix 𝐀 i \mathbf{A}_{i} , our proposed method spends all computation and communication resources of the client on matrix 𝐁 i \mathbf{B}_{i} .

Freezing client matrices 𝐀 i \mathbf{A}_{i} to their initial value saves computational and communication resources at the cost of a lower model utility [ 11 , 12 ] . To balance efficiency and utility, we propose resampling and freezing 𝐀 i \mathbf{A}_{i} matrices at each round. This approach avoids the gradient coupling noise found in existing resampling strategies—like FLoRA [ 10 ] —where both matrices are fine-tuned simultaneously. Consequently, our method cuts clients’ overhead by half, eliminates gradient interference between 𝐀 i \mathbf{A}_{i} and 𝐁 i \mathbf{B}_{i} , and mitigates the low-rank limitations of LoRA . Finally, we demonstrate that per-round resampling and freezing of 𝐀 i \mathbf{A}_{i} approximates full fine-tuning under rank-dependent gradient perturbations, characterized by gradient scaling and additive noise. The signal-to-noise ratio ( SNR ) of perturbed gradients increases with the adaptation rank r r . Therefore, clients with heterogeneous ranks experience varying levels of gradient perturbation. This variance renders a uniform learning rate suboptimal. We thus also propose rank-dependent learning rate adjustments to compensate for this heterogeneity and achieve further performance improvement. Our main contributions are summarized below: • We introduce SPRA-LoRA , a federated fine-tuning framework for rank-heterogeneous environments. By resampling and freezing client 𝐀 i \mathbf{A}_{i} matrices, it cuts computation and uplink communication costs by 50% while mitigating LoRA’s low-rank constraints.

• SPRA-LoRA employs rank-aware learning rates for clients to account for their different levels of gradient perturbation. This tailored approach stabilizes training, leading to faster convergence and superior performance compared to the existing methods using uniform learning rates. • We provide a convergence proof for SPRA-LoRA in non-convex settings, accounting for variations in rank, data and system resources. Our analysis demonstrates that SPRA-LoRA is fundamentally equivalent to performing Fed-Avg on adapters with noisier batch gradients. • Experimental results across multiple models and language tasks show that SPRA-LoRA improves utility and convergence speed with 50% less computation and uplink communication overhead on clients compared to state-of-the-art baselines.

LoRA is a prominent PEFT method for federated fine-tuning [ 13 ] . Recent work highlights the asymmetry between its component matrices 𝐀 \mathbf{A} and 𝐁 \mathbf{B} : Zhu et al. [14] evaluates freezing 𝐀 \mathbf{A} versus 𝐁 \mathbf{B} , while Hayou et al. [15] improves performance using matrix-specific learning rates. Recent work by Lee et al. [16] demonstrates that optimizing the learning rate significantly boosts the performance of LoRA . Kalajdzievski [17] studies the impact of the scaling factor s s on the learning process of LoRA . chunks.section: 2.1 Federated LoRA with homogeneous client ranks
chunks.text: The first category of research assumes homogeneous resources where all n n clients use a uniform rank r r , with matrices { 𝐀 i } ∈ ℝ r × m \{\mathbf{A}_{i}\}\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times m} and { 𝐁 i } ∈ ℝ n × r \{\mathbf{B}_{i}\}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times r} . Early methods like SLoRA [ 18 ] , FedIT [ 8 ] , and FeDeRA [ 20 ] independently apply FedAvg to these components. However, this causes client-side gradient coupling noise from simultaneous update of the components [ 12 ] and server-side aggregation noise [ 9 , 10 ] . To reduce coupling, LA-LoRA [ 12 ] and RoLoRA [ 11 ] use alternating optimization, though separate component aggregation still incurs noise. LoRA-A 2 [ 25 ] extends this with mask-based adaptive rank selection. Conversely, FFA [ 22 ] and LoRA-FA [ 28 ] freeze { 𝐀 i } \{\mathbf{A}_{i}\} to aggregate only { 𝐁 i } \{\mathbf{B}_{i}\} for improved stability at the cost of model utility. While FedSA-LoRA [ 24 ] aggregates only { 𝐀 i } \{\mathbf{A}_{i}\} —claiming it learns general global knowledge—we show that 𝐀 i \mathbf{A}_{i} acts primarily as a random projection for gradients rather than a knowledge-capturing parameter. Finally, EcoLoRA [ 26 ] and FLASC [ 21 ] focus on communication efficiency via segment sharing and sparsity. The aforementioned algorithms aggregate { 𝐀 i } \{\mathbf{A}_{i}\} and { 𝐁 i } \{\mathbf{B}_{i}\} separately, making them limited to homogeneous ranks and vulnerable to the aggregation noise [ 9 , 10 ] .

chunks.section: 2.2 Federated LoRA with heterogeneous client ranks
chunks.text: Varied client resources often require heterogeneous ranks r i r_{i} , causing dimension mismatches in { 𝐀 i } ∈ ℝ r i × m \{\mathbf{A}_{i}\}\in\mathbb{R}^{r_{i}\times m} and { 𝐁 i } ∈ ℝ n × r i \{\mathbf{B}_{i}\}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times r_{i}} that prevent direct component aggregation. To resolve this, HetLoRA [ 19 ] uses zero-padding with sparsity-weighted aggregation, while [ 23 ] employs replication-based padding; both require matrix truncation for redistribution. FSLoRA [ 27 ] uses a fixed global rank and separate aggregation of components on the server side, and each client uses sketching to update submatrices of the global LoRA modules. While addressing rank heterogeneity, the fixed global rank limits FSLoRA ’s rank heterogeneity. Aggregating components separately and fine-tuning them simultaneously, all three methods suffer from the aggregation and coupling noises. FlexLoRA [ 9 ] and FLoRA [ 10 ] avoid the aggregation noise by aggregating reconstructed updates { Δ 𝐖 i = s i 𝐁 i 𝐀 i } ∈ ℝ n × m \{\Delta\mathbf{W}_{i}=s_{i}\mathbf{B}_{i}\mathbf{A}_{i}\}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times m} . FlexLoRA then redistributes components through computationally expensive truncated SVD of the aggregated update. FLoRA implements the update aggregation by stacking clients’ LoRA components and avoids the SVD by merging the aggregated update into clients’ local adapters and reinitializing both the LoRA matrices for the next round. Yet, both FLoRA and FlexLoRA still suffer from the coupling noise, due to simultaneous fine-tuning of LoRA components.

chunks.section: 2.2 Federated LoRA with heterogeneous client ranks
chunks.text: In contrast, by treating { 𝐀 i } \{\mathbf{A}_{i}\} as periodically resampled, frozen random projection matrices and fine-tuning only { 𝐁 i } \{\mathbf{B}_{i}\} , SPRA-LoRA totally eliminates the gradient coupling noise as well as the aggregation noise, while halving clients’ overhead. This random- 𝐀 \mathbf{A} framework paves the way to precisely quantify a rank-dependent gradient perturbation existing in LoRA dynamics, leading to a theoretically grounded strategy where clients adapt their learning rates based on their specific ranks. Unlike heuristic alternatives, our approach accelerates convergence and improves model utility.

Our previous findings suggest that rather than applying a uniform learning rate—a standard practice in all previous Fed-LoRA methods—clients should employ learning rates tailored to their specific ranks. Applying a single, global learning rate forces some clients to operate outside their ideal operation zone, leading to diminished performance compared to their rank-specific optimum.

Rather than applying a uniform learning rate across the entire clusters, our rank-aware SPRA-LoRA framework ensures that clients within each cluster j j utilize a specific learning rate optimized to maximize fine-tuned model utility for that specific rank. chunks.section: 5.2 Rank-aware learning rate selection for SPRA-LoRA
chunks.text: To determine the optimal learning rate η r i \eta_{r_{i}} for individual ranks, we propose the following simple strategy: Each cluster of clients with a common rank performs federated fine-tuning and an intra-cluster evaluation over a grid of cluster-specific learning rates. Note that this method has no additional communication overhead compared to existing baselines. Additionally, when using SGD optimizer, the square law η r ∗ = η c ​ r 2 \eta_{r}^{*}=\eta_{c}r^{2} could be used to further diminish the overhead of learning rate tuning.

In this section, we prove the convergence of SPRA-LoRA in non-convex settings under mild assumptions. Let us define global objective function f ⁡ ( 𝐖 ) := ∑ i = 1 n f i ​ ( 𝐖 ) / n f(\mathbf{W}):=\sum_{i=1}^{n}f_{i}(\mathbf{W})/n , with minimum value f ⋆ f^{\star} and minimizer 𝐖 ∗ \mathbf{W}^{*} . We also make some mild assumptions about the loss functions f i f_{i} , including their Lipschitz continuity and smoothness (see Assumptions G.1 in the Appendix).

We evaluate our approach on language generation and understanding tasks using LLaMA-3.2-3B [ 38 ] (on Commonsense Reasoning dataset [ 39 ] ) and RoBERTa-base [ 40 ] (on GLUE benchmark [ 41 ] ). Considering our heterogeneous-rank setting, only the baselines highlighted in blue in Table 1 are the main baselines comparable to SPRA-LoRA . Yet, we extend the aggregation strategies of the recent algorithms FedSA [ 24 ] , RoLoRA [ 11 ] and LA-LoRA [ 12 ] with zero padding (similar to HetLoRA [ 19 ] ) and use them as baselines as well. Also, we generalize the aggregation strategy of FFA to aggregate { Δ 𝐖 i e = s i 𝐁 i e , T 𝐀 i e , 0 } \{\Delta\mathbf{W}_{i}^{e}=s_{i}\mathbf{B}_{i}^{e,T}\mathbf{A}_{i}^{e,0}\} at the end of each round e e (instead of aggregating { 𝐁 i e , T } \{\mathbf{B}_{i}^{e,T}\} ) to extend it to settings with heterogeneous client ranks. For Commonsense Reasoning (GLUE), data is partitioned across n = 20 n=20 ( n = 40 n=40 ) clients with a Dirichlet distribution with α = 2 \alpha=2 ( α = 0.8 \alpha=0.8 ) by default [ 10 , 9 , 27 ] . Client ranks are sampled uniformly and non-uniformly from { 4 , 8 , … , 128 } \{\texttt{4},\texttt{8},\dots,\texttt{128}\} , with identical configurations applied to all baselines to ensure a fair comparison. We use a cluster with 4 NVIDIA H100 80 GB GPUs for running our experiments. Each experiment is run on a single GPU. Further details about our experimental setup is explained in Appendix A.1 .

The Commonsense benchmark results, detailed in Tables 3 and 3 , compare uniform and log-normal client rank distributions across three SPRA-LoRA variants: a uniform learning rate version designed to isolate the effects of per-round resampling and weight freezing against the FFA baseline, the standard rank-aware learning rate configuration, and a "double-rank" alternative. Despite 50% lower overhead, SPRA-LoRA with a uniform learning rate matches or exceeds most baselines. Its significant performance advantage over FFA stems from its per-round resampling strategy. Both the methods share the same number of trainable parameters, and the marginal increase in run time for SPRA-LoRA reflects the time for per-round parameter merging, saving and reloading in our experiments, rather than increased computational complexity. HetLoRA suffers from both aggregation noise (due to aggregating 𝐀 \mathbf{A} and 𝐁 \mathbf{B} matrices separately) and coupling noise (due to simultaneous optimization of 𝐀 \mathbf{A} and 𝐁 \mathbf{B} matrices). While FLoRA shares SPRA-LoRA ’s per-round resampling and resetting strategy, it still suffers from the coupling noise, due to fine-tuning both the component matrices simultaneously with a uniform learning rate. In contrast, SPRA-LoRA demonstrates superior performance by resampling and freezing { 𝐀 i e , 0 } \{\mathbf{A}_{i}^{e,0}\} and utilizing rank-aware learning rates for clients. Remarkably, SPRA-LoRA achieves these gains while reducing computational and communication overhead by 50% compared to FLoRA and other baselines.

To avoid coupling noise, LA-LoRA and RoLoRA alternately optimize 𝐀 \mathbf{A} and 𝐁 \mathbf{B} between local steps and rounds, respectively, matching the computational overhead of SPRA-LoRA . However, SPRA-LoRA outperforms them by treating 𝐀 \mathbf{A} as a resampled random projection matrix and allocating the full computational budget to 𝐁 \mathbf{B} . This is motivated by the fact that with zero-initialized 𝐁 \mathbf{B} , matrix 𝐀 \mathbf{A} remains nearly frozen during fine-tuning ( Section 4 , Lemma B.1 in Appendix, and [ 34 ] ). Table 4 : Average test accuracy (5 runs) on GLUE language understanding benchmark with Dirichlet distribution ( α = 0.8 \alpha=0.8 ), RoBERTa model and AdamW optimizer. Clients’ ranks follow uniform distribution over { 4 , 8 , … , 128 } \{\texttt{4},\texttt{8},\dots,\texttt{128}\} . SPRA-LoRA and its doubled-rank variant outperform baselines while maintaining 50% less or equal client overhead, respectively.

FedSA performs the weakest. By training both 𝐀 \mathbf{A} and 𝐁 \mathbf{B} locally while aggregating only 𝐀 \mathbf{A} on the server, it leaves 𝐁 \mathbf{B} local. Hence, clients never receive an aggregated 𝐁 \mathbf{B} matrix. This necessitates strict full client participation [ 24 ] . Furthermore, because each client maintains a personalized model, FedSA ’s results are averaged across random seeds and clients. As shown, under partial participation, the overall performance for FedSA is low and there is a high variance across clients (large std s). Finally, to ensure a fair comparison, the final row of results evaluates SPRA-LoRA with doubled client ranks to match the trainable parameters and overhead of the baselines. Under these equivalent resource constraints, SPRA-LoRA achieves its most significant performance gains, highlighting its superior efficiency and utility. Similar trends are observed for the GLUE benchmark in Table 4 . SPRA-LoRA ’s gains derive from per-round resampling of 𝐀 \mathbf{A} matrices, focusing computational resources on optimizing 𝐁 \mathbf{B} matrices and rank-aware heterogeneous learning rates. This approach avoids both aggregation and coupling noises. Convergence results in Figure 5 demonstrate that both variants of SPRA-LoRA consistently achieve higher average test accuracy across the GLUE benchmark throughout the communication rounds compared to the baselines. Figure 6 shows an ablation study on data heterogeneity ( α \alpha ) and number of clients ( n n ), with consistently superior performance of SPRA-LoRA variants. See Appendix A.2 for detailed results. Finally, Table 5 examines T T (local steps for SPRA-LoRA and matrix 𝐀 \mathbf{A} resampling period). Using a centralized setting ( r = 64 r=64 , 1000 steps with AdamW ) to isolate federated optimization effects, we find minimal difference between T > 1 T>1 and T = 1 T=1 for small T T , showing negligible impact from the weak dependence between matrices 𝐀 \mathbf{A} and batch gradients. Appendix F proves that per- T T -steps resampling introduces a bounded mean shift to per-step sampling ( Lemma 4.1 ), decaying with T T .

We proposed SPRA-LoRA to address update scale imbalances across heterogeneous client ranks. By freezing and resampling matrices 𝐀 \mathbf{A} and applying rank-scaled learning rates, SPRA-LoRA balances gradient perturbations for superior efficient performance. Future work will explore dynamic rank adaptation and continuous learning rate schedules.

The goal of this paper is to advance the field of Machine Learning. Our paper is foundational research and not tied to any particular application with negative impacts. There are many potential societal consequences of our work, none which we feel must be specifically highlighted here.

We provide more details about our experiments in this section.

In all experiments, we sample client ranks from { 4 , 8 , 16 , 32 , 64 , 128 } \{\texttt{4},\texttt{8},\texttt{16},\texttt{32},\texttt{64},\texttt{128}\} . For each training experiment, we run 5 seeds and report the mean and sample standard deviation ( std ) across them. We use p = 0.2 p=0.2 participation rate, uniform batch size of b i = 16 b_{i}=16 , and AdamW optimizer. Next, we describe specific configuration choices for the GLUE and Commonsense reasoning benchmarks. GLUE. The GLUE benchmark is a collection of natural language understanding tasks, formatted as classification tasks with 2 or 3 classes [ 41 ] . We randomly initialize and freeze the classification layer of a RoBERTa-base model. We then apply rank-stabilized LoRA (rs- LoRA ) with α = 1 \alpha=1 to the ["query", "value", "key", "dense"] parameters, where the first three refer to the attention input projections and “dense” is the second-to-last fully connected layer (before the final classifier layer). We use a maximum sequence length of 128 tokens. We tune learning rate over { 1e-4 , 2e-4 , 4e-4 , 1e-3 , 2e-3 , 4e-3 } \{\texttt{1e-4},\texttt{2e-4},\texttt{4e-4},\texttt{1e-3},\texttt{2e-3},\texttt{4e-3}\} and select the best performing learning rate based on the average across all 7 benchmarks. We use the same grid of learning rates when searching for the client-specific ranks for SPRA-LoRA . We do an ablation study on the GLUE benchmark with varying data heterogeneity (Dirichlet parameter α \alpha ) and number of clients ( n n ), as shown in Table 6 . chunks.section: Theorem C.3 (Classical Central Limit Theorem: [ 43 ] , Theorem 27.1) .
chunks.text: Suppose that { X i } i = 1 n \{X_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n} , is an independent sequence of random variables having the same distribution with mean μ \mu and positive variance σ 2 \sigma^{2} . Define S n = ∑ i = 1 n X i S_{n}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}X_{i} as their sum. Let Z n Z_{n} be defined by Z n = S n − n ​ μ n ​ σ . Z_{n}=\frac{S_{n}-n\mu}{\sqrt{n}\sigma}. Then, the distribution of Z n Z_{n} approaches standard normal distribution as n n approaches infinity. The theorem above states that S n S_{n} is approximately, or asymptotically, distributed as a normal distribution with mean n ​ μ n\mu and variance n ​ σ 2 n\sigma^{2} . The next theorem is about the Lindeberg’s condition, which is a sufficient (and under certain conditions also a necessary condition) for the Central Limit Theorem (CLT) to hold for a sequence of independent random variables { X i } i = 1 n \{X_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n} . Unlike the classical CLT stated above, which requires the sequence of random variables to have a finite variance and be both independent and identically distributed ( i.i.d ), Lindeberg’s CLT only requires the sequence of random variables to have finite variance, be independent and also satisfy the Lindeberg’s condition. The following states the theorem.

chunks.section: Theorem C.4 (Lindeberg and Lyapounov Theorem: [ 43 ] , Theorem 27.2) .

chunks.section: Appendix E Extension of Lemma 4.1 to Kaiming-Uniform initialization of { 𝐀 ℓ } ℓ = 1 L \{\mathbf{A}_{\ell}\}_{\ell=1}^{L}
chunks.text: We now extend the result derived in Lemma 4.1 to Kaiming-Uniform initialization of { 𝐀 ℓ } ℓ = 1 L \{\mathbf{A}_{\ell}\}_{\ell=1}^{L} to show that a similar rank-dependent behavior exists. Kaiming uniform initialization [ 31 ] , is primarily designed for neural networks employing ReLU -like activation functions. While it was originally derived for ReLU , its principles can be extended to other non-linear activations like GELU , which is a smoother variant of ReLU . The core idea of Kaiming initialization is to set the initial weights in a way that helps maintain a consistent variance of activations throughout the network, preventing vanishing or exploding gradients during training. For uniform distribution, the weights are drawn from a uniform distribution within a specific range 𝒰 ⁡ ( − b , b ) \mathcal{U}(-b,b) , where b = 6 / m b=\sqrt{6/m} . The value of b b is found for each layer such that the variance of each subsequent pre-activation layer is equal, e.g. in Figure 1 , the variance of each element in y y is equal to that of each element in the pre-activation of input x x . Building on these foundations, we introduce SPRA-LoRA ( S tochastic P rojection and R ank- A ware LoRA ), a federated rank-aware fine-tuning strategy that utilizes frozen, resampled 𝐀 \mathbf{A} matrices and rank-dependent learning rates for clients. We also prove its convergence with heterogeneous client resources. Our experiments across benchmark datasets demonstrate that SPRA-LoRA consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines with half the overhead on clients.
